title: Oak & Furrows Wildlife Rescue (Swindon & Cricklade)
location: Blakehill Nature Reserve, Malmesbury Road, Cricklade, SN6 6RH
summary: Primary wildlife rehabilitation hospital serving Swindon and North Wiltshire. Admits over 4,000 casualties annually including hedgehogs, badgers, foxes, birds, and small mammals.
advice: If you find an injured or grounded animal, call before moving it if safe to do so.
Containment: Gently place the casualty in a cardboard box lined with an old towel or newspaper. Ensure ventilation holes are punched from inside out.
Keep the animal in a warm, dark, and quiet room away from children and household pets.
Never offer cow's milk, bread, or forced water to a distressed wild animal.

title: Wiltshire Wildlife Hospital
summary: 24-hour voluntary emergency response and rehabilitation for injured wildlife across Wiltshire, dealing with deer, raptors, badgers, swans, and water birds.
advice: Operates a 24-hour wildlife emergency mobile line; if unanswered immediately, send a text message with location details and casualty description.
For road casualty deer or badgers, do not approach an agitated animal directly; keep traffic safe and call for experienced rescuers.
Keep casualties warm and calm during transit.

title: RSPCA National Cruelty & Emergency Helpline
summary: National 24-hour reporting line for wild animals trapped in dangerous machinery, waterways, wire netting, or suffering suspected deliberate cruelty.
advice: Use for trapped wildlife or when local rescue centres are unreachable.
Have what3words, GPS coordinates, or a precise landmark ready when calling.
Request an incident reference number to track response.

title: Bat Conservation Trust - National Bat Helpline
summary: Authoritative national helpline for grounded, injured, or trapped bats, building work queries, and roost protections.
advice: Any bat found grounded or exposed during daylight is in trouble and needs containment.
Safety: Always wear protective gardening gloves when touching a bat; never handle bare-handed.
Containment: Place a shoe box or small container over the bat, slide a piece of stiff card underneath, and secure with a tight lid with small air holes.
Put a clean bottle cap containing a few drops of water in the corner so it can drink if able.

title: Badger Protection & Wildlife Crime Reporting
summary: Legal framework under the Protection of Badgers Act 1992 and protocols for reporting sett interference, persecution, or illicit earth-stopping.
advice: The Law: It is a criminal offence to wilfully kill, injure, take, ill-treat a badger, or damage, destroy, block, or disturb an active sett.
Sett Discretion: Precise coordinates must never be published online, on open maps, or in public forums to guard against persecution.
Emergency: If a wildlife crime or sett interference is taking place now, call 999 immediately.
Reporting: Call Wiltshire Police on 101, ask for the Wildlife Crime Officer, and obtain an incident log number.
Anonymous reports: Call Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111.

title: Nesting Birds & Hedgerow Protection
summary: Statutory protection for all wild birds, active nests, eggs, and countryside hedgerows.
advice: All wild birds, their active nests, and eggs are protected under Section 1 of the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981.
It is an offence to intentionally take, damage, or destroy the nest of any wild bird while it is being built or in active use.
No Hedge Cutting: Do not trim hedges, scrub, or trees during the core nesting season between 1 March and 31 August.
Hedgerow Regulations 1997: Countryside hedgerows over 20 metres in length require council consent prior to removal.

title: Caring for Hedgehogs & Garden Corridors
summary: Practical ways to support garden hedgehogs, establish linked corridor highways, provide safe food, and identify casualties.
advice: What to Feed: Meat-based dog or cat wet food (chicken or beef), specialized hedgehog biscuits, or meat-based cat crunchies.
Water: Always provide fresh water in a shallow, stable dish. Water is vital during dry summer spells.
Lethal Foods: NEVER offer cow's milk or bread. Hedgehogs are lactose intolerant; milk causes severe dehydration and fatal enteritis.
Daylight Sightings: Hedgehogs are strictly nocturnal. Any hedgehog seen wandering in daylight, wobbling, coughing, or surrounded by flies is unwell and needs urgent rescue.
Autumn Hoglets: Any juvenile hedgehog weighing under 450 grams after late October lacks the fat reserves to survive winter hibernation and should be brought to Oak & Furrows.
Hedgehog Highway: Create a 13cm x 13cm (5x5 inch) hole at the base of boundary fences so hedgehogs can forage across their necessary 2km nightly range.

title: Feeding Garden Birds & Feeder Hygiene
summary: Guidance on nutritional bird foods by season, feeder safety standards, and preventing the spread of avian diseases.
advice: Recommended Foods: Sunflower hearts (high energy, no waste husks), nyjer seeds (for finches), pinhead oatmeal, and live/dried mealworms.
High-Energy Winter Feeding: Calorie-dense suet cakes and fat blocks are essential during cold snaps.
Remove Netting: ALWAYS remove and discard plastic mesh nets from fat balls before hanging; mesh snags bird claws and causes leg amputation.
No Loose Peanuts in Spring: Never put loose whole peanuts in feeders during breeding season (April-July); parent birds may feed them to chicks, causing choking.
Feeder Hygiene: Avian trichomonosis and salmonella spread rapidly at dirty feeding stations. Clean feeders and tables weekly with pet-safe disinfectant.
Disease Break: If sick, lethargic, or fluffed-up greenfinches/chaffinches are seen, suspend feeding and bird baths for 2 to 3 weeks to break contagion.

title: Badgers: Diet, Responsible Feeding & Water
summary: Understanding natural badger ecology, seasonal feeding realities, and avoiding habituation or nuisance in residential areas.
advice: Natural Diet: Earthworms form over 50% of a badger's natural food intake, supplemented by beetles, acorns, bulbs, roots, and fallen orchard fruit.
Do They Need Feeding?: Badgers are resourceful foragers and rarely need supplementary feeding. Over-feeding causes dependency and can attract rats.

Safe Supplementary Foods: During prolonged summer droughts or hard ground frosts when earthworms cannot be reached, small amounts of raw unsalted peanuts, kibbled maize, or apple/pear slices may be provided.
What NOT to Feed: Never leave raw meat, bones, cooked poultry, bread, or sweet confectionery. These cause digestive illness and conflict with domestic pets.
Ground Water: Keep a heavy, shallow ceramic dish of fresh tap water at ground level. Clean and refill daily.

title: Wildlife Ponds, Escape Ramps & Drought Water
summary: Designing wildlife-friendly garden ponds, preventing small mammal drownings, and maintaining clean water sources during heatwaves.
advice: Sloping Banks: Always ensure at least one side of a pond has a shallow, gently sloping stone or pebble beach. This enables hedgehogs, frogs, and emerging dragonflies to climb out safely.
Escape Ramps: For existing steep-sided ponds, rain butts, or cattle troughs, install a rough wooden plank or wire ramp wrapped in hessian.
No Fish in Wildlife Ponds: Ornamental fish (goldfish, koi) consume amphibian eggs, tadpoles, and aquatic insect larvae.
Native Oxygenators: Plant native Hornwort (Ceratophyllum demersum) and Water Crowfoot. Never introduce invasive alien weeds like Crassula helmsii or Floating Pennywort.
Bird & Pollinator Saucers: Place shallow glazed dishes at ground level and elevated on pedestals. Place flat stones in the center so drinking bees and butterflies cannot submerge.

title: Insects, Pollinators & Nectar Plants
summary: Selecting high-yield native plants, managing verges for pollinators, maintaining deadwood, and phasing out harmful chemical pesticides.
advice: Continuous Nectar Calendar: Plant flowers that bloom sequentially from March through October (e.g. Primrose, Pulmonaria, Bird's-foot Trefoil, Field Scabious, Knapweed).

Ivy is Vital: Mature flowering ivy (Hedera helix) in September to November is the single most critical late nectar and pollen source for hoverflies, solitary bees, and butterflies preparing for winter.
Deadwood Habitats: Retain log piles and decaying wood in damp, shady garden corners. Deadwood supports over 2,000 UK insect species including stag beetles.
No Mow May & Relaxed Verges: Leaving grass to flower until late summer allows clover, dandelions, and trefoils to feed thousands of pollinators.
Pesticide Elimination: Avoid all chemical slug pellets (metaldehyde/ferric phosphate), weedkillers, and neonicotinoid pesticides, which bioaccumulate and kill thrushes, frogs, and hedgehogs.
